title: Sex Ed

jokes.text: Dwight approaches day laborers speaking broken Spanish, recruiting them for work
jokes.setup: Dwight approaches Spanish-speaking men at a day labor site, attempting to communicate in broken Spanish to recruit a worker
jokes.punchline: His mangled Spanish ('Necesito un bueno worker. Tu es fuerte.') reveals his delusion that he's multilingual and authoritative
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight character comedy — his pompous confidence in broken Spanish fits his self-aggrandizing persona perfectly. Functional opener but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Day laborers warn each other about Dwight: 'We don't go with that man. I've seen several men go with that man and none come back.'
jokes.setup: Day laborers huddle and warn each other about the strange man (Dwight) approaching them for work
jokes.punchline: The description makes Dwight sound like a serial killer, played with complete sincerity by the laborers
jokes.explanation: The joke works because the laborers' deadpan terror reframes Dwight as genuinely sinister. 'None come back' delivered straight is funnier than any exaggeration. Good structure and dark edge.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional: reveals he has Mose impersonate an INS agent to kidnap day laborers, dump them in Harrisburg and tell them it's Canada
jokes.setup: We've been watching Dwight recruit day laborers for seemingly legitimate work
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals an elaborate scheme involving fake INS agents, kidnapping, and geographic deception — Harrisburg being passed off as Canada is the absurdist peak
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalating specificity ('by the name of Mose Schrute,' 'tells them it's Canada') is perfectly structured. Deeply character-specific — only Dwight has a cousin Mose, only Dwight would conceive this scheme and casually confess it to a documentary crew. The detail of Harrisburg-as-Canada is inspired absurdism. Earns a high score because the escalation is meticulous and the character integration is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: New hire reveals he's from 'la Philadelphia' — he's a fluent English speaker from Pennsylvania, not an immigrant
jokes.setup: Dwight is interrogating a Spanish-speaking man about his origins, continuing his elaborate immigration charade
jokes.punchline: 'Scranton. Y... before that, la Philadelphia.' He speaks perfect English. Dwight's entire scheme collapses into mundanity.
jokes.explanation: Efficient misdirection payoff — the extended Spanish charade collapses beautifully when the man casually reveals he's just a local guy. 'Scranton' landing as a punchline is economical and sharp. Good structure.

jokes.text: Nate attempts to deal with a hornet's nest using a blowtorch, then a bat — chaos ensues with people fleeing and screaming 'They're stinging him!'
jokes.setup: Dwight has left new maintenance worker Nate to deal with a hornet's nest with 'all the tools he needs,' framing it as 'do or die'
jokes.punchline: Nate first reaches for a blowtorch (people panic), then settles on a bat to beat the nest — getting swarmed. The escalating panic from bystanders drives the comedy.
jokes.explanation: Solid physical escalation sequence. 'Interesting choice' from Dwight as Nate reaches for the bat is the comedic peak. Dwight's detached commentary as observer elevates what could be generic slapstick. Loses points for being somewhat predictable in direction.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional about Nate choosing between tools: 'This is do or die. If he chooses correctly, he'll conquer the hornets. And if he doesn't? He'll die.'
jokes.setup: Dwight frames Nate's hornet-nest removal as a life-or-death trial
jokes.punchline: When asked what happens if he doesn't choose correctly, Dwight answers with complete seriousness: 'He'll die'
jokes.explanation: Dwight's total sincerity about employee mortality is funny and in-character. The structure is clean — the 'do or die' phrase is set up as a platitude and then Dwight takes it literally. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael enters asking Erin for 'any mustaches, I mean messages' while wearing a fake mustache
jokes.setup: Michael enters the office wearing a fake mustache
jokes.punchline: He slips and says 'mustaches' instead of 'messages,' immediately correcting himself, revealing he's self-conscious about it
jokes.explanation: The Freudian slip is a nice economical joke, and the fake mustache as setup is inherently funny. Works as a scene-setter but not exceptional on its own.

jokes.text: Michael's confessional explaining why a man would wear a fake mustache: 'He is a fan of the outrageous. He loves to surprise! He loves other things as well.'
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining — seemingly in earnest — the various reasons a man might wear a fake mustache to work
jokes.punchline: 'He loves other things as well' — the trailing non-answer is the joke; he's out of reasons and won't admit he just felt like it
jokes.explanation: The confessional format lets Michael's self-justification hang in the air. 'He loves other things as well' is a perfectly deflating non-ending. Good economy, solid character voice.

jokes.text: Michael: 'It's a pimple, Phyllis. Avril Lavigne gets them all the time, and she rocks harder than anyone alive.'
jokes.setup: Someone (Phyllis) has noticed something on Michael's face — he has a cold sore / herpes
jokes.punchline: Michael's defense is to invoke Avril Lavigne as a peer and role model, which is both delusional and hilariously specific
jokes.explanation: This is a great Michael Scott joke. The Avril Lavigne reference is perfectly specific — she's not an A-lister, she's not obviously cool, which makes Michael's earnest invocation of her all the funnier. 'She rocks harder than anyone alive' as an unshakeable conviction about a pop-punk teenager is deeply in character. High originality, high character integration, very quotable.

jokes.text: After Phyllis hints it might be something serious, Michael leaps to: 'You mean cancer?'
jokes.setup: Phyllis says the thing on Michael's face is 'no pimple,' hinting it might be something else
jokes.punchline: Michael's first guess is cancer — skipping all intermediate diagnoses
jokes.explanation: Quick, economical joke. Michael's catastrophizing personality means 'cancer' is a believable first jump. Not surprising given the character but executed efficiently.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'It's just good to catch a Michael train of thought early before it derails and destroys the entire town.'
jokes.setup: Jim is commenting on the office's need to redirect Michael's thinking when he starts catastrophizing
jokes.punchline: The metaphor escalates from 'derails' to 'destroys the entire town' — the hyperbole is perfectly dry
jokes.explanation: Jim's confessional deadpan at its best. The train metaphor starting logically and then catastrophizing to 'the entire town' mirrors the very Michael behavior being described. Self-referential structure is elegant. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Meredith casually announces she has herpes — 'I have it myself. That's what it is. I've never seen herpes on you. 'Cause it's on my genitals, genius.'
jokes.setup: The office is debating whether Michael's cold sore is herpes; Meredith chimes in with expertise
jokes.punchline: 'Cause it's on my genitals, genius' — delivered completely straight, as if the question was stupid
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The economy is exceptional — two words ('my genitals') do enormous work. Meredith's complete lack of shame or self-awareness, treating the questioner as the fool for not knowing, is perfectly in character and delivered with devastating flatness. 'Genius' as the capper elevates it further. Could only be Meredith — near-perfect character integration. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Michael asks 'You have a penis?' after Meredith says herpes is on her genitals
jokes.setup: Meredith says her herpes is on her genitals
jokes.punchline: Michael mishears or misunderstands and asks if she has a penis — his brain doesn't compute 'female genitals'
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist beat. Michael's obliviousness is the joke. Works in the moment but relies more on shock than craft. The setup/punchline ratio is efficient.

jokes.text: The office debates Michael's age: 'That was, like, 10 years ago.' / 'No, it was, like, four years ago.' / 'Michael, you're at least 46.' / 'Why "at least"? If you're guessing 46, just say 46.'
jokes.setup: Michael mentions his last STD test was at his physical when he was 40
jokes.punchline: The office argues about how long ago that was, implying he's older than he admits. Michael's objection isn't to the age but to the hedge — 'why at least?' — revealing his vanity
jokes.explanation: The final beat — Michael not caring about being 46 but offended by 'at least' — is a precise character joke. It reveals his vanity and self-delusion in one economical exchange. Well-structured multi-person beat.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'Can we please talk about how gross Meredith is?'
jokes.setup: The Meredith herpes revelation has just occurred
jokes.punchline: Angela's response isn't about the situation's implications — it's pure personal disgust. The 'please' adds prissy formality.
jokes.explanation: Angela's talking head is economically perfect — six words, completely in character, no wasted syllables. The prissy indignation of 'can we please' captures Angela in one breath. High character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight confessional: 'This is what you get when you treat your body like an outhouse.'
jokes.setup: Dwight commenting on Meredith's herpes revelation
jokes.punchline: 'Outhouse' as the metaphor — rustic, functional, humiliating — is a very Dwight word choice
jokes.explanation: The word 'outhouse' does all the work. It's agrarian, judgmental, and distinctly Dwight. Efficient character joke.

jokes.text: Andy: 'The number one sexually transmitted disease is ignorance.'
jokes.setup: Andy jumps in to calm the Meredith slut-shaming, citing his R.A. credentials
jokes.punchline: His earnest PSA platitude — 'the number one STD is ignorance' — lands as self-parody because he's clearly just reciting an R.A. talking point with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Andy's oblivious earnestness with his R.A. background is good character work. The platitude is funny because he believes it completely. Sets up his later sex-ed plotline nicely.

jokes.text: 'I guess maybe she could marry a meth dealer with crabs...'
jokes.setup: Office members are speculating about Meredith's future romantic prospects given her health situation
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'meth dealer with crabs' as the best-case scenario is darkly hilarious
jokes.explanation: The joke works on specificity — not just a bad person, but a 'meth dealer with crabs.' The descending logic (Meredith can only attract someone equally compromised) is mean but funny. Loses points for unclear attribution.

jokes.text: Michael's confessional: 'You know what? I feel like one of those old-timey sailors with VD. (in gruff voice) Eh, it's me own darn fault. Girl in every port! What port? The Jan port? The Holly port?'
jokes.setup: Michael is processing how he might have gotten herpes, running through his sexual history
jokes.punchline: He adopts a salty-sailor voice to play-act his own debauchery, then the 'ports' become his ex-girlfriends — revealing the sad reality that his 'ports' are just Jan and Holly
jokes.explanation: This joke has real craft. Michael's grandiose self-mythologizing (the sailor voice) punctured by the tiny reality (he's only been with Jan and Holly) is deeply character-specific. The physical comedy of the voice acting, the sadness underneath, and the naming of 'ports' are all excellent. The joke earns its length.

jokes.text: Michael calls Donna to notify her of potential herpes exposure, spelling out 'H-I' — Donna panics thinking it's HIV — then completes: 'R-P-E-E-S'
jokes.setup: Michael calls an ex to notify her of possible herpes. He says 'I can't even say it. H-I...' — the pause lets the audience and Donna think HIV
jokes.punchline: 'R-P-E-E-S' — he spells herpes wrong and inadvertently terrified her with HIV implications first
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the HIV misdirect is set up naturally because Michael is genuinely trying to be circumspect. 'R-P-E-E-S' (misspelled) as the resolution delivers a double joke: relief from HIV scare plus Michael can't even spell herpes correctly. Smart, well-timed, good emotional stakes.

jokes.text: Michael to Donna: 'I am calling to see if you gave me herpes, because if you did, I would be able to avoid a lot of sucky conversations.'
jokes.setup: Michael is supposed to be notifying Donna of possible herpes exposure
jokes.punchline: Instead of being contrite, he's essentially accusing her and framing it as an administrative convenience for himself
jokes.explanation: Michael's self-centered inversion — making a public health notification about his personal convenience — is perfectly in character. 'Sucky conversations' as the motivation is honest and revealing.

jokes.text: Andy's attention-request debate: Michael points out Andy has asked for everyone's attention 'like a year ago' and Andy protests, triggering everyone to cite specific occasions (new phone, World Cup scores)
jokes.setup: Andy asks for everyone's attention to address Meredith's situation; Michael says 'Not again'
jokes.punchline: The office collectively remembers all the times Andy has commandeered their attention — World Cup scores, new phone — building a picture of Andy's neediness
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble beat that uses the full office to paint Andy's character. 'The world's only international sport' as Andy's defensive justification for the World Cup scores is a nice character touch.

jokes.text: Michael calls Holly — gets a man, says 'This is Holly.' Man corrects him. Michael says again 'This is Holly.' Man corrects again. Finally: 'No... This is Michael Scott.'
jokes.setup: Michael nervously calls Holly's number; a man picks up and Michael mistakes him for Holly
jokes.punchline: Michael keeps saying 'This is Holly' when he means 'Is this Holly?' — the correction reveals he's been identifying himself as Holly, not asking for her. 'Busted.' lands from Dwight.
jokes.explanation: The repeated misfire — 'This is Holly' — is a good structural joke with escalating absurdity. Dwight's 'Busted' as the observation is a perfect one-word reaction. Michael's nervous confusion is believable.

jokes.text: Michael on the phone with Holly: 'Any nuns?' / 'Three nuns.' / 'Missionaries from South Africa.' / 'Were they in the missionary position?' — Holly laughs
jokes.setup: Holly is telling Michael about a terrible car accident she made up as a pretext to call
jokes.punchline: Michael adds 'Were they in the missionary position?' — a terrible pun that Holly laughs at anyway, revealing their chemistry
jokes.explanation: The pun itself isn't exceptional, but what makes this work is Holly laughing — it's doing double duty as a joke AND a character/relationship beat. The fact that she finds his dumb pun funny tells us everything about why they belong together. High character integration for a middling pun.

jokes.text: Andy sings an improvised pizza jingle to lure colleagues into his sex-ed session: 'Hot pizza, check it and see / I got a whole bunch of pepperoni'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to get colleagues to participate in a sex-ed presentation he's organized
jokes.punchline: He resorts to singing an off-brand jingle — a parody of 'Hot Blooded' — about pizza as a bribe, revealing how desperate he is for participation
jokes.explanation: Andy's show-tune impulse as a solution to social awkwardness is on-brand. The Foreigner parody is recognizable but not particularly clever. Works as characterization more than as a joke.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly phone conversation: 'We would have twins.' / 'I don't think we'd have kids. We dated for a few weeks.' / 'We would be married.'
jokes.setup: Holly asks if Michael ever wonders what life would have been like if she hadn't transferred
jokes.punchline: Michael's fantasy (twins, marriage) clashes against Holly's reality (a few weeks of dating) in a rapid-fire alternating exchange that reveals his delusion
jokes.explanation: The rapid alternation between Michael's romantic fantasy and Holly's grounded reality is structurally tight and very funny. 'Twins' as his first fantasy is perfectly over-the-top. The economy is excellent — the joke is in the juxtaposition itself, needing no additional commentary.

jokes.text: Holly: 'Michael, you cried at that tag line for a movie you made up. "He had no arms or legs. He couldn't see, hear or speak. This is how he led a nation."'
jokes.setup: Holly is arguing that Michael romanticizes things and projects emotions onto situations
jokes.punchline: As proof, she recounts that he cried at a tagline for a FICTIONAL movie he invented himself — and the tagline describes an impossible person (no arms, legs, sight, hearing, or speech) leading a nation
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and one of the great Michael Scott jokes ever written. Every layer works: (1) He cried at a movie tagline. (2) It was a movie he made up. (3) The tagline describes a person with literally no sensory or physical capability. (4) 'This is how he led a nation' delivered as inspirational. The specificity of every detail (not just 'a sad movie' but a SELF-INVENTED movie with an IMPOSSIBLE protagonist) is extraordinary. Perfect character integration — only Michael would do all of this. Highly quotable, instant rewatch classic. Comparable in quality to the 9+ anchor examples.

jokes.text: Dwight whispering to camera after Michael's Holly call: 'He forgot to mention the herpes.' Michael: 'It didn't come up organically.'
jokes.setup: Michael just had a long, flirtatious call with Holly but never mentioned the herpes notification he was supposed to deliver
jokes.punchline: Dwight's aside to camera names the elephant in the room; Michael's defense — 'it didn't come up organically' — is absurd given he could have just said it
jokes.explanation: 'It didn't come up organically' applied to a required herpes notification is perfectly absurd. Michael's social delusion on display in six words. Dwight's whisper-to-camera is a nice mockumentary moment.

jokes.text: Jan has released an album of Doris Day covers on her own label. Michael doesn't get the reference when she sings the 'Enjoli' commercial jingle.
jokes.setup: Jan is presenting herself as a successful supermom — raising her daughter, directing purchasing, releasing music
jokes.punchline: She sings the 'Enjoli' commercial ('Bring home the bacon, fry it up in a pan, never let you forget you're a man') — a deeply ironic song for someone in a toxic past relationship — and Michael says 'I don't understand the reference'
jokes.explanation: Jan releasing Doris Day covers on her own label is a perfectly Jan detail — aspirational, tone-deaf, grandiose. Michael not getting the commercial reference is consistent. The irony of the 'Enjoli' lyrics about supporting a man, coming from Jan, is a nice layered touch for attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Dwight asks if there's an operating theater open to visitors, then wanders off to find one
jokes.setup: Michael and Jan need a private moment at the hospital; Dwight has accompanied Michael
jokes.punchline: Dwight's response to being dismissed is to seek out a surgical theater to observe — treating the hospital as an attraction
jokes.explanation: A quick but satisfying character beat. Only Dwight would treat the hospital as a tourist destination and seek out surgery to watch. Jan's 'He hasn't changed' is the perfect punctuation.

jokes.text: Jan: 'Michael Scott, you are here for a post-mortem. You wanna dig into our relationship, go over it, see what killed it.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Jan if he's the kind of person who misremembers relationships as more than they were
jokes.punchline: Jan, a master of directness, immediately names what he's actually doing — a 'post-mortem' — cutting through Michael's obfuscation with clinical precision
jokes.explanation: Jan's psychoanalytic precision is perfectly in character. 'Post-mortem' is a great word choice — medical enough to fit the hospital setting, clinical enough to deflate Michael's romanticism. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Andy's sex-ed class: shows photos of genitalia to the office. 'What, 'cause he's black?' / 'Nope. It's 'cause it's genitalia.'
jokes.setup: Andy shows an image of genitalia to the class; the office recoils in disgust
jokes.punchline: Jim (Tuna) asks if the objection is because of race. Andy clarifies it's because it's genitalia — a classically absurd reversal of sensitivity.
jokes.explanation: The race/genitalia confusion is sharp — it inverts expected PC concerns and catches the audience off guard. Andy's 'Perfectly normal genitalia, Tuna' delivery makes it funnier. High impact in a group viewing context.

jokes.text: Andy shows second STD-afflicted genital photo: 'Yeah, sure, it's got some herpes on it. But you know what? It's just as normal as anyone else's.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to destigmatize herpes; he shows a photo of herpes-afflicted genitalia
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, sure, it's got some herpes on it. But you know what? It's just as normal as anyone else's.' — his forced positivity about a medical condition while the office is visibly horrified
jokes.explanation: Andy's relentless positivity in the face of a horrified audience is good cringe comedy. 'Just as normal as anyone else's' about a diseased organ is a nice ironic inversion of what 'normal' means.

jokes.text: Jan's analysis of her relationship with Michael: 'Well, there was a bit of a learning curve in the conversation department, but between the sheets, we were like Jordan and Pippen.'
jokes.setup: Michael claims he and Jan were 'not good' at the beginning of their relationship
jokes.punchline: Jan casually rates the sex as 'Jordan and Pippen' level — a jarring, weirdly specific sports metaphor from someone as prim as Jan
jokes.explanation: Jan using a Bulls metaphor for sex — when she's the furthest thing from a sports person — is the joke. The specificity of 'Jordan and Pippen' (not just 'great teammates') implies she's thought about this and chosen carefully, which makes it weirder and funnier.

jokes.text: Jan's 'princess' allegory: Michael asks 'Am I the princess?' Jan: 'No, I'm the princess. And the queen.' Michael: 'So I'm the guy at the station.'
jokes.setup: Jan explains their dynamic via a princess/queen allegory in which she was attracted to Michael partly to defy her own better judgment
jokes.punchline: Michael hopefully asks if he's the princess; Jan corrects that she's both princess and queen — leaving Michael as 'the guy at the station,' a non-character, a prop in his own love story
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character joke. Jan claiming BOTH princess AND queen in her own allegory — while Michael is 'the guy at the station' — perfectly captures their power dynamic and Jan's narcissism. Michael's resigned acceptance of his diminished role is quietly heartbreaking and funny. High originality in how it uses the allegory structure.

jokes.text: Jan is singing an improvised song to her daughter Astrid (Assie); mid-song, Michael announces 'I have herpes.'
jokes.setup: Jan is in a warm, musical moment with her young daughter, singing about what she might have learned at school
jokes.punchline: Michael blurts 'I have herpes' mid-lullaby — destroying the maternal scene with the information he's been struggling to deliver all episode
jokes.explanation: Outstanding comic timing and structure. The warmth of the lullaby scene makes the interruption maximally disruptive. 'I have herpes' as a three-word bomb into a children's song is about as good a punchline delivery as this episode gets. The economy (nine words of warm singing, three words of chaos) is exceptional. Earns a high score.

jokes.text: Andy's sex-ed pros/cons list: Kevin contributes 'It feels unbelievable.' Andy asks if that's different from 'feels amazing.' Kevin: 'Yes.' Andy writes it down.
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to lead an adult sex-ed discussion, starting with pros of sex
jokes.punchline: Kevin insists 'feels unbelievable' and 'feels amazing' are distinct categories; Andy, genuinely uncertain, writes both down — both playing it completely straight
jokes.explanation: Kevin's earnest insistence on the distinction — and Andy respecting it — is good ensemble comedy. Both characters playing it straight is the key. Kevin's particular investment in the nuances of sexual pleasure is on-brand.

jokes.text: Creed: 'The feeling of pure risk.' — submitted as a pro of sex. Andy had it in the cons column; Creed says 'It's thrilling' and Andy moves it.
jokes.setup: Andy is taking pro/con submissions about sex from the office
jokes.punchline: Creed identifies 'the feeling of pure risk' as a sexual pro — revealing his dangerous, borderline sociopathic relationship with sex; his one-word justification 'It's thrilling' is perfectly Creed
jokes.explanation: Creed's character is built entirely on implications of crimes and lifestyle choices the show never explains. 'The feeling of pure risk' as a sexual value — said with complete calm — is exactly the right kind of Creed joke. The fact that Andy initially had it in the cons column (correct!) and Creed persuades him otherwise with just 'It's thrilling' is perfectly economical. High character integration.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's baby called an 'unplanned pregnancy' — 'Just admit that your baby was a mistake.' / 'She was a surprise.' / 'I'm sure they don't regret having that child. Let's move it to the pros.'
jokes.setup: Andy names unplanned pregnancy as a con of sex; the room notes Jim and Pam
jokes.punchline: Andy/room forces Jim and Pam to publicly defend their daughter's conception; 'She was a surprise' is accepted as sufficient to move it to pros
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat that uses Jim and Pam as reluctant participants in Andy's chaos. 'She was a surprise, not a mistake' is a real parental distinction that lands here as both funny and sweet. Andy moving it to pros based solely on their mild protest is good logic comedy.

jokes.text: Michael and Dwight in the car: 'To have the ability to point out if a man is making a bigger deal out of something than is really there.' 'Wait, what Holly said?' 'Yes!' 'I don't... Forget it, Michael. Today is about herpes.'
jokes.setup: Michael is seeking Dwight's input on whether he romanticizes relationships
jokes.punchline: Dwight tries to redirect Michael back to the herpes mission; when Michael almost engages, Dwight aborts: 'Forget it. Today is about herpes.' — treating herpes as the more manageable topic
jokes.explanation: 'Today is about herpes' as a focusing mantra is funny because herpes is now the pragmatic, sensible topic relative to Michael's emotional issues. Good character dynamic.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'And who is going to pay.' — added as a third objective after Michael lists who gave him herpes and who has it
jokes.setup: Michael says 'today is about who gave it to me, who has it...'
jokes.punchline: Dwight appends 'and who is going to pay' — reframing the public health mission as vengeance
jokes.explanation: Dwight's threat of retribution, delivered as a calm addendum, is perfectly economical. It's consistent with his earlier monologue about 'taking overwhelming revenge' on whoever gave you a disease. Good callback energy even without formal callback structure.

jokes.text: Dwight yelling navigation: 'Left! Willow, now!' as Michael apparently misses the turn, with car horn blaring.
jokes.setup: Dwight is navigating for Michael; Michael is distracted by conversation
jokes.punchline: Dwight's escalation from calm instruction to screaming 'Left! Willow, now!' with a car horn implies Michael nearly caused an accident
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy — Dwight's panic about Michael's driving is consistent with their dynamic. Not particularly crafted; it's a transitional comedic beat rather than a real joke.

jokes.text: Michael and Dwight arrive at an elderly care facility; Michael mistakes the wrong woman for Helene and tells Dwight to 'take my grandmother for a walk' — Dwight leads the confused old lady away
jokes.setup: Michael is looking for his ex Helene at what appears to be a nursing home or care facility
jokes.punchline: He mistakes an elderly woman for Helene and has Dwight detain her: 'Take my grandmother for a walk while I talk to the real Helene.' Dwight complies without question.
jokes.explanation: The visual of Dwight briskly walking away with a confused elderly woman is strong physical comedy. Michael calling her 'my grandmother' (not even getting her name right) is the right level of callous obliviousness. Dwight's unquestioning compliance is in perfect character.

jokes.text: Andy's sex-ed lesson: 'What's the safest way to go skiing? Don't ski.' (office laughs) Andy: 'I just thought I'd bring it up in case someone here was practicing abstinence.'
jokes.setup: Andy claims abstinence is the only true safe sex — a straight-faced pitch to a room of adults
jokes.punchline: The skiing analogy lands a laugh, but Andy's follow-up — checking if anyone present is practicing abstinence — is the real joke, implying he might be
jokes.explanation: The skiing analogy is the kind of thing an earnest R.A. would think is devastating logic. The follow-up about abstinence — implying Andy might be the target of his own lesson — adds a layer of character self-revelation.

jokes.text: Andy demonstrates condom use on a pencil. Oscar: 'Why would you choose a pencil, Andy?' Andy: 'Well, I'm not gonna use my penis, Oscar. It's not exactly hard right now, anyway.'
jokes.setup: Andy announces he'll demonstrate putting on a condom using 'this pencil'
jokes.punchline: Oscar's objection to the pencil (implying there are better props) leads Andy to explain he's not using his penis — then volunteer that it 'isn't exactly hard right now anyway,' an overshare that devastates the room
jokes.explanation: This is a standout moment. The escalation from 'pencil' to 'my penis' to 'it's not exactly hard right now, anyway' is textbook escalating overshare. Andy volunteering his current level of arousal to defend his teaching method — completely missing the point of Oscar's objection — is excellent character comedy and earns a high impact score. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Meredith has a reaction (presumably the condom demonstration goes wrong) — 'It'll go away in time. Just don't touch it.' — implying the condom broke or something went wrong
jokes.setup: Andy is demonstrating condom use on a pencil in the office conference room
jokes.punchline: Meredith's reaction — 'Whoa!' — and Andy's response 'It'll go away in time. Just don't touch it.' implies a catastrophic demonstration failure
jokes.explanation: The inferred visual gag works — we don't see what happens, but 'Don't touch it' implies a snapped pencil or burst condom. Functional cringe beat but somewhat dependent on what's happening visually.

jokes.text: Helene to Michael: 'I think that for you to have come here even expecting that we could have a conversation like this shows how self-deluded you are. Michael, your memory has failed you greatly.' Michael's response: 'Jerk.'
jokes.setup: Helene has just delivered a withering psychological assessment of Michael's relationship with memory and self-image
jokes.punchline: 'Jerk.' — Michael's only response to a sophisticated and devastating critique is a single word, a child's insult
jokes.explanation: One of the most economical jokes in the episode. Helene delivers a PhD-level assessment of Michael's psychology. Michael's rebuttal is 'Jerk.' The comic collapse from sophisticated argument to playground insult is pure Michael Scott — he can't process the critique and defaults to a child's response. Perfect economy (one word), perfect character integration. Earns high scores.

jokes.text: Michael arrives at a house for sale, finding Carole — his realtor ex — showing it. He pretends he 'pulled in' randomly when she clearly had him tracked down through her office.
jokes.setup: Michael shows up at Carole's open house as if by coincidence
jokes.punchline: Carole reveals her receptionist told her 'a man called but would only say he was my ex-lover' — and Michael tries to maintain the coincidence fiction
jokes.explanation: 'He would only say that he was my ex-lover' is a funny detail — Michael couldn't even give his name, just the relationship descriptor. His subsequent 'That's so... Weird. Yeah.' cover-up attempt is thin and funny.

jokes.text: Andy-Erin confrontation: Andy quotes his own proposal to Erin verbatim: 'My good sir, nothing would make me happier than to hand you the hand of the hand once in my hand.'
jokes.setup: Andy is confronting someone about asking Erin out after Andy supposedly approved
jokes.punchline: He quotes himself with perfect precision on a sentence that makes no grammatical sense: 'hand you the hand of the hand once in my hand' — five 'hands' — while treating this as a clear and binding agreement
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional joke. 'Hand you the hand of the hand once in my hand' is genuinely inspired nonsense — it sounds like it should mean something because of the grammatical structure, but it's pure word salad with 'hand' repeated five times. Andy quoting it verbatim with pride, as if it was a beautiful, clear statement, is perfect character comedy. Extremely quotable, high originality.

jokes.text: 'The only reason I said that is 'cause you asked me so politely, and it was very difficult for me to say no.'
jokes.setup: Andy is confronted with his own impossible-to-parse approval of someone dating Erin
jokes.punchline: He admits he only gave permission because he was asked politely — revealing that 'hand you the hand of the hand once in my hand' was a politeness capitulation, not a genuine blessing
jokes.explanation: Good follow-through on the previous joke, but functions mainly as a button rather than a standalone joke. Andy's politeness being weaponized against him is characterful.

jokes.text: Carole showing the house: 'You put the TV there. You put your family here.' — Michael's response to seeing a family room
jokes.setup: Carole is touring Michael through the house; they find a second living room ('It's a family room')
jokes.punchline: Michael's analysis: 'You put the TV there. You put your family here.' — a completely utilitarian, slightly sad reduction of domestic life
jokes.explanation: A quick, understated joke with mild melancholy. Michael's reductive view of family life as a spatial arrangement is economical and slightly revealing.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I'm between specialists right now.' — responding to Carole asking if a doctor has checked his cold sore
jokes.setup: Carole, concerned about Michael's cold sore (herpes), asks if a doctor has seen it
jokes.punchline: 'I'm between specialists right now' — treating the total absence of a doctor with the language of a busy executive managing multiple professionals
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy joke. 'Between specialists' implies he has SO MANY specialists that there's always a gap between them — when in reality he has none. The corporate/executive language applied to personal health avoidance is very Michael. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Carole: 'Yes. Actually, you do make a bigger deal out of things than you need to. You proposed to me on our fourth date.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Carole if he romanticizes things
jokes.punchline: 'You proposed to me on our fourth date' — confirming his pattern with devastating specificity and casualness
jokes.explanation: The fourth-date proposal is a funny data point that confirms Michael's pattern across multiple relationships. Carole's matter-of-fact delivery is perfect — she's not angry, just stating a fact.

jokes.text: Dwight in Carole's house: 'Excuse me. Someone died in the upstairs bathroom, didn't they?' Carole: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been wandering the house while Michael and Carole talk
jokes.punchline: Dwight emerges with a very specific real estate concern — whether someone died in the bathroom — framed as a potential dealbreaker
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical Dwight joke. His non-sequitur investigation of the house, landing on bathroom death as his primary concern, is exactly what Dwight would do. 'Didn't they?' implies he has circumstantial evidence. Carole's flat 'No.' is the correct straight-man response. Very Dwight.

jokes.text: Crying-but-not-crying stranger gives Michael life advice: 'I'm sweating... Man up, all right? Son, you will win this in the end. It's all about heart and character.' Talking head: 'I have no idea what his problem is. It's just my standard advice.'
jokes.setup: Michael encounters a crying man in Carole's house who insists he isn't crying
jokes.punchline: The man delivers an inspirational speech to Michael (a stranger) as if Michael is the one who needs help — then confessional: 'I have no idea what his problem is. It's just my standard advice.'
jokes.explanation: The reverse therapy joke — the clearly distressed man giving unsolicited life advice as 'standard' — is a good absurdist premise. 'It's just my standard advice' implies he distributes this speech indiscriminately. Works as a one-off character.

jokes.text: An old man (stranger) finds Michael crying/sweating outside. 'Are you crying?' / 'No, I'm just sweating.' / 'I don't know what's got you upset, but my advice is stop crying.'
jokes.setup: Michael is outside the house, visibly emotional after his conversations
jokes.punchline: A random old man dispenses some of the most useless advice in television history: 'Stop crying.' Then adds: 'Man up. Son, you will win this in the end.'
jokes.explanation: The stranger's useless-but-sincere pep talk ('stop crying' as actionable advice) is a nice absurdist beat. His talking-head afterward — 'I have no idea what his problem is. It's just my standard advice. It's good advice, right?' — adds a layer of comedy by revealing this is his regular routine.

jokes.text: Stranger's talking-head: 'I have no idea what his problem is. It's just my standard advice. It's good advice, right?'
jokes.setup: The stranger has just given Michael generic pep talk advice
jokes.punchline: He reveals in a confessional that (a) he has no idea what Michael's problem is, (b) he gives this same speech to everyone, and (c) he's slightly uncertain it's even good
jokes.explanation: The mockumentary format is used well here — giving a talking-head to a one-scene character who dispenses generic wisdom and then admits he doesn't know anything about the situation. The uncertainty of 'It's good advice, right?' is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Michael's voicemail to Holly: '...it was mostly a freak show. And you and me, that must have been a real train wreck... Holly, you're wrong. You are wrong.'
jokes.setup: Michael has left emotional voicemail for Holly reflecting on his day of visiting ex-girlfriends
jokes.punchline: His phrasing — 'mostly a freak show' as a description of his exes, followed immediately by insisting his relationship with Holly was different — is the joke: he's using terrible language to argue for romantic sincerity
jokes.explanation: The humor in the voicemail comes from Michael's tone-deafness in the framing — 'freak show' is a harsh description of people he dated, and it transitions clumsily into his romantic argument for Holly. Emotionally genuine despite the verbal fumbling, which is classic Michael.

jokes.text: Michael's voicemail to Holly: 'Today, I ended up seeing a lot of the women that I used to date, and in my mind, they were all great. And then when I actually saw them, it was mostly a freak show.'
jokes.setup: Michael is leaving Holly a heartfelt voicemail about his day visiting his exes
jokes.punchline: 'It was mostly a freak show' — his unvarnished assessment of his own dating history, delivered mid-romantic declaration
jokes.explanation: The pivot from romantic introspection to 'mostly a freak show' is well-timed. Michael's honesty here is both self-aware (about his own poor taste) and still somewhat insulting to the women. The qualifier 'mostly' is doing quiet work. Character voice is strong.

jokes.text: End of heartfelt Holly voicemail: 'Oh, and you might, you should talk to a doctor because you might have herpes. Bye.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just left the most sincere, moving romantic declaration of the episode to Holly's voicemail
jokes.punchline: He appends the herpes notification as a casual afterthought — 'Oh, and... Bye.' — the entire episode's A-plot reduced to a postscript
jokes.explanation: One of the two best jokes in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: Michael reaches an emotional crescendo (the genuine romantic declaration) and then the entire episode's mission — notifying Holly of possible herpes — becomes 'Oh, and...' The 'Bye.' after 'you might have herpes' is pitch-perfect anticlimactic punctuation. This rewards everyone who watched the full episode. Exceptional callback, exceptional economy, exceptional structure. Comparable to the 9+ anchor examples.

jokes.text: Michael tells Oscar he needs to inform him that they may have exchanged an STD from their public kiss — 'Herpes duplex. It's probably just an ingrown mustache hair, but we have to be exhaustive.'
jokes.setup: Michael tracks down Oscar as his last ex-'lover' — referencing their forced public kiss during a previous episode's diversity presentation
jokes.punchline: 'Herpes duplex' (not the real name), immediately hedged by 'it's probably just an ingrown mustache hair, but we have to be exhaustive'
jokes.explanation: 'Herpes duplex' as a made-up medical term is a good detail — Michael has clearly been reading about this. The immediate self-undermining ('probably just an ingrown mustache hair') is excellent character comedy — he's simultaneously alarming and reassuring Oscar in the same breath. 'We have to be exhaustive' as a public health posture is very funny.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'We were never lovers.' Michael: 'I'm gonna need a list of every man you've ever had sex with. I'm talking train stations, men's rooms...'
jokes.setup: Oscar protests that he and Michael were never lovers — just forced to kiss for a diversity presentation
jokes.punchline: Michael ignores this and asks for a comprehensive list of Oscar's sexual history — then begins listing stereotypical gay cruising locations ('train stations, men's rooms') as prompts
jokes.explanation: Michael's list of Oscar's presumed sexual locations is ignorant in a very Michael way — he's not being malicious, he's just reciting what he thinks Oscar's life looks like, based on stereotypes. Sets up the escalating list to follow.

jokes.text: The escalating list of locations where Oscar supposedly had sex: 'Flower shops, fireworks celebrations... Fence with a hole in it. Moonlit gondola. Carriage ride through Central Park. The woods behind the liquor store. Electric car dealership. The Democratic Primary.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Dwight are helping Oscar remember his sexual encounters by listing increasingly absurd locations
jokes.punchline: The list begins with gay stereotype locations ('fence with a hole in it') and escalates through romantic clichés ('moonlit gondola,' 'carriage ride through Central Park') to completely surreal additions — 'electric car dealership' and 'the Democratic Primary'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's highlights. The list is structured with escalating absurdity: it starts with crude gay stereotypes (fence with a hole), moves through oddly romantic locations (gondola, Central Park), then lands on 'electric car dealership' — completely random — and finally 'the Democratic Primary' — which implies organized sexual activity at a political event. The ending is the kind of left-field absurdism that makes the best Office list jokes. Michael and Dwight contributing as if they're genuinely helping is perfect. Highly quotable and rewatchable.

tmdb_overview: Michael, believing he has herpes, contacts all his ex-girlfriends, including Jan and Holly. Andy tries to play on Erin’s compassionate side by holding a sex education meeting for the office.
